convex-optimization-doubt-log.idea: Choose the best allowed answer. Convexity makes that search easier because every local minimum is global.
convex-optimization-doubt-log.caption: The objective ranks answers; constraints decide which answers are allowed. Learn the geometry before choosing a solver.

cards.title: Objective
cards.text: A score to minimize, such as cost, error, or energy.

cards.title: Feasible set
cards.text: All choices that satisfy the constraints. A convex set contains every segment joining two of its points.

cards.title: Convex problem
cards.text: A convex objective, convex inequality functions, and affine equality constraints.

convex-optimization-doubt-log.note: A convex objective alone is not enough: the feasible set must also be convex.
rows: Study PSD matrices and quadratic programs.
Move to second-order and semidefinite cones.

linear-algebra-important-concepts.idea: A matrix moves space. Eigenvectors reveal unchanged directions; SVD reveals how any matrix rotates, stretches, and rotates again.
linear-algebra-important-concepts.visual: See a matrix act on space
linear-algebra-important-concepts.caption: A = diag(2, 1) doubles horizontal lengths. The unit circle becomes an ellipse; the coordinate axes remain eigenvector directions.

cards.title: Columns are instructions
cards.text: The columns of A are where the coordinate basis vectors land.

cards.title: Eigenvectors keep direction
cards.text: Av = λv: the vector stays on its line, with scaling or reversal set by λ.

cards.title: SVD works broadly
cards.text: A = UΣVᵀ separates input directions, stretching, and output directions, including for rectangular matrices.

linear-algebra-important-concepts.note: For this diagonal example, the singular values are 2 and 1. The largest is the maximum length gain.
rows: Try an eigenbasis if the matrix is diagonalizable.
Use singular values and singular vectors.

shannon-information-entropy-doubt-log.idea: Surprise belongs to one outcome. Entropy averages that surprise over all possible outcomes.
shannon-information-entropy-doubt-log.visual: A fair coin is hardest to predict
shannon-information-entropy-doubt-log.caption: For a binary source, uncertainty peaks at p = ½. When either outcome is certain, no bits are needed to describe which outcome occurred.

cards.title: Rare means surprising
cards.text: An outcome with probability 1/8 carries 3 bits of self-information.

cards.title: Average the surprise
cards.text: A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy; a biased coin has less.

cards.title: Coding uses the bias
cards.text: Frequent outcomes can receive shorter codes, lowering average length over long sequences.

shannon-information-entropy-doubt-log.note: The logarithm turns multiplication of independent probabilities into addition of information.
rows: Heads: 0.152 bits; tails: 3.322 bits; average: 0.469 bits.

symmetric-matrices-quadratic-forms-matri.idea: A symmetric matrix assigns curvature to directions. Its eigenvectors give the axes; its eigenvalues tell you how strongly each axis contributes.
symmetric-matrices-quadratic-forms-matri.caption: For A = diag(4, 1), the set xᵀAx ≤ 1 has horizontal radius ½ and vertical radius 1. More curvature means a shorter ellipse axis.

cards.title: Quadratic form
cards.text: xᵀAx turns a vector into a scalar energy or curvature score.

cards.title: PSD means every direction
cards.text: A is positive semidefinite when xᵀAx ≥ 0 for every x, equivalently all eigenvalues are nonnegative.

cards.title: Norm means largest gain
cards.text: The matrix 2-norm is the largest singular value: the greatest length amplification over unit inputs.

symmetric-matrices-quadratic-forms-matri.note: This eigenvector expansion applies to real symmetric A. Positive definite matrices give bounded ellipsoids.
rows: A bowl; bounded ellipsoidal sublevel sets.
A flat direction; PSD but potentially singular.
A saddle; the quadratic is not convex.

classical-machine-learning-models-from-f.idea: Choose a model by the shape of the problem: predict a value, separate classes, group examples, or find a smaller representation.
classical-machine-learning-models-from-f.caption: These are schematic examples: a regression line predicts a number, a decision boundary separates labels, and clusters group nearby points.

cards.title: Start with an assumption
cards.text: Linear models use additive effects; trees split feature space; kernels express similarity.

cards.title: Control flexibility
cards.text: Regularization trades training fit for a simpler model. Ridge shrinks weights; lasso can set them to zero.

cards.title: Evaluate the consequence
cards.text: Choose held-out metrics that reflect the cost of mistakes, then choose a threshold if needed.

classical-machine-learning-models-from-f.note: Fit preprocessing on training data only. Use validation to choose settings; reserve the test set for final evaluation.
rows: Linear regression is a useful baseline.
Use K-means for groups or PCA for variance-preserving projection.

deep-learning-field-notes.idea: Training is a feedback loop: predict, measure error, send gradients backward, and update parameters. Every layer has a job in that loop.
deep-learning-field-notes.caption: The forward pass builds a prediction. Backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse; the optimizer uses those gradients to update weights.

cards.title: Loss defines the target
cards.text: Cross-entropy scores class probabilities. Focal loss reduces the contribution of already easy examples.

cards.title: Layers move information
cards.text: Convolutions mix local patterns, activations add nonlinearity, and normalization controls selected statistics.

cards.title: Training differs from inference
cards.text: Dropout samples masks in training. BatchNorm usually uses running statistics at inference; LayerNorm uses each example.

deep-learning-field-notes.note: This is plain gradient descent. Adam also tracks moving averages of gradients and their squares.
rows: Check targets, gradients, and a tiny-batch overfit.
Inspect data leakage, distribution shift, and overfitting.
Measure on the target device before pruning or quantizing.

generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.idea: Generative models learn how data can arise from hidden variables. A VAE learns a compact latent code; diffusion learns to reverse gradual corruption.
generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.visual: Two routes from noise to data
generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.caption: A VAE decoder maps a latent sample to data in one pass. Diffusion generation repeatedly denoises; its forward corruption process is fixed.

cards.title: Posterior inference
cards.text: Given x, infer which latent z could have produced it. Exact inference is often intractable.

cards.title: VAE shortcut
cards.text: Train an encoder q(z|x) and decoder together using reconstruction and a KL regularizer.

cards.title: Diffusion shortcut
cards.text: Create noisy examples at known noise levels, then train a model to predict the chosen denoising target.

generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.equation: \log p(x)\geq\mathbb E_{q(z\mid x)}[\log p(x\mid z)]-D_{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))
generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.note: The ELBO rewards explaining the observation while penalizing disagreement with the prior.
rows: Use z = μ + σ ⊙ ε with independent standard Gaussian ε.
Sample its noise level directly; no full forward chain is needed.
Use a frozen image codec, then train diffusion in its latent space.
generative-ai-variational-inference-vaes.next_title: The VAE as an image codec

probability-statistical-inference-for-ma.idea: Probability predicts data from a model. Likelihood scores models using observed data. Bayes combines likelihood with a prior.
probability-statistical-inference-for-ma.visual: Update a belief after observing data
probability-statistical-inference-for-ma.caption: Starting with Beta(2, 2), observing 8 heads and 2 tails yields Beta(10, 4). The posterior combines prior evidence and observed counts.

cards.title: Probability
cards.text: Hold the parameter fixed and ask which data could occur.

cards.title: Likelihood
cards.text: Hold the observed data fixed and compare parameter values. It need not integrate to one over parameters.

cards.title: Posterior
cards.text: Multiply likelihood by prior, then normalize over the parameter space.

probability-statistical-inference-for-ma.note: For a Bernoulli probability, a Beta(a, b) prior becomes Beta(a + heads, b + tails).
rows: MLE maximizes likelihood; MAP maximizes posterior density.
It measures tail extremeness under the null model, not the probability the null is true.
Correlation measures association; it does not establish causation.

vae-training-for-latent-diffusion.idea: Before training diffusion, check whether the VAE can reconstruct the details you care about. The codec limits what the generator can recover.
vae-training-for-latent-diffusion.visual: Find the bottleneck before scaling the model
vae-training-for-latent-diffusion.caption: Encode a real image and decode it immediately. If that reconstruction already loses a feature, increasing denoiser capacity cannot recover that feature through this fixed codec.

cards.title: Spatial capacity
cards.text: Latent height and width determine how much spatial detail survives. Extra channels are a different kind of capacity.

cards.title: Balanced objective
cards.text: Reconstruction preserves information; KL regularization structures the posterior. Inspect both terms separately.

cards.title: Freeze the contract
cards.text: Save the VAE checkpoint, latent shape, scaling, and choice of posterior mean or sample with the diffusion setup.

vae-training-for-latent-diffusion.note: At decode time, undo any latent normalization before passing latents to the VAE decoder.
rows: Fix the codec before tuning diffusion.
KL is near zero, reconstructions are poor
Check whether the decoder is ignoring the latent.
Check latent scaling and denoiser/sampler agreement next.

why-kl-annealing-helps-vaes.idea: Let the VAE learn to use its code before charging the full price for storing information. Warmup changes the learning path, while the final KL weight sets the trade-off.
why-kl-annealing-helps-vaes.visual: First open the channel, then regularize it
why-kl-annealing-helps-vaes.caption: A rising β gradually adds KL pressure. In the scalar experiment, an overly large final β still makes zero information optimal; warmup cannot remove that incentive.

cards.title: Reconstruction wants information
cards.text: Encoder and decoder must learn together so z actually explains x.

cards.title: KL charges for information
cards.text: Strong pressure too early can push the encoder toward an input-independent prior.

cards.title: Annealing changes timing
cards.text: Begin with a small β, raise it toward a chosen target, and keep checking reconstruction and latent use.

why-kl-annealing-helps-vaes.note: β is meaningful relative to the reconstruction loss scale and its sum-versus-mean reduction.
rows: Inspect decoder dependence on z; consider a slower warmup.
Revisit the final objective and KL weight.
Inspect scaling, reductions, and reconstruction before changing β.

training-latent-diffusion-models.idea: Diffusion learns the distribution of your encoded images. Make the codec, latent scale, prediction target, and reverse sampler agree before adding complexity.
training-latent-diffusion-models.visual: Training and generation run in different directions
training-latent-diffusion-models.caption: Training samples one noise level and predicts a target. Generation starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly applies a compatible reverse sampler before decoding.

cards.title: Freeze a working codec
cards.text: Confirm real-image reconstructions and record whether training uses means or posterior samples.

cards.title: Create one noisy latent
cards.text: Draw a timestep and Gaussian noise, then compute zₜ directly from the clean latent.

cards.title: Match the sampler
cards.text: Epsilon, clean-latent, and velocity prediction require the matching conversion equations and schedule.

training-latent-diffusion-models.note: Training timesteps define noise levels. Sampling steps are a separate choice and may use a subset of those levels.
rows: Use a simple unconditional model and fixed sample seeds.
Apply the same convention in training and sampling, and undo it for decoding.
Loss falls, samples do not improve
Check interfaces and timestep-specific error before adding capacity.

conditioning-and-scaling-latent-diffusio.idea: Send a condition through a path that preserves its structure: labels are global, masks are spatial, and text is a token sequence.
conditioning-and-scaling-latent-diffusio.visual: Put the condition where it can help
conditioning-and-scaling-latent-diffusio.caption: A label can modulate features, a spatial map can be concatenated or injected at multiple scales, and tokens can provide keys and values for cross-attention.

cards.title: Global information
cards.text: Embed class labels or scalar metadata and use the embedding to influence denoiser blocks.

cards.title: Spatial information
cards.text: Keep masks or maps aligned with the image through resizing and augmentation.

cards.title: Guidance needs training
cards.text: Classifier-free guidance requires training with some conditions dropped so unconditional predictions are meaningful.

conditioning-and-scaling-latent-diffusio.note: Here s = 0 gives the unconditional estimate and s = 1 gives the conditional estimate. Larger values strengthen guidance, with possible quality trade-offs.
rows: Use an embedding and feature modulation.
Use aligned spatial features or concatenation.
Use cross-attention; queries come from image features.

debugging-latent-diffusion-training.idea: Debug the simplest deterministic boundary first. A lower denoising loss alone cannot tell you which part of the image pipeline is working.
debugging-latent-diffusion-training.caption: Check the codec, scaling, a tiny-set overfit, sampler agreement, and evaluation in that order. Move onward when the previous boundary behaves as expected.

cards.title: Lock the comparison
cards.text: Reuse validation latents, timesteps, noise, and generation seeds to make changes comparable.

cards.title: Separate training from sampling
cards.text: Compare raw and EMA weights with identical generation settings. Bucket denoising loss by noise level.

cards.title: Resume the experiment
cards.text: Restore model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, EMA, step count, and needed random states.

debugging-latent-diffusion-training.note: Use the table to choose the first check. Change one component at a time so the result identifies a cause.
rows: Targets, gradients, timestep inputs, and conditioning.
Missing optimizer, scheduler, EMA, or random state.

latent-diffusion-training-series.idea: Build a reliable pipeline, add control, then evaluate systematically. Start at the earliest part whose assumptions you have not yet verified.
latent-diffusion-training-series.caption: Each stage has a clear exit check. The VAE codec is a prerequisite shared by all three parts.

cards.title: 01 · Build
cards.text: Understand latent encoding, noise schedules, prediction targets, and reverse sampling.

cards.title: 02 · Control
cards.text: Add the right condition path; scale model capacity after the baseline works.

cards.title: 03 · Diagnose
cards.text: Use fixed comparisons, tiny-set overfitting, and complete checkpoints.

latent-diffusion-training-series.note: The VAE, normalization, target, schedule, conditions, and sampler form one shared contract.
rows: Part 1: Training Latent Diffusion Without Guesswork.

cnn-vs-transformer-why-conformer-needs-b.idea: Speech has nearby acoustic patterns and distant context. Conformer gives convolution and attention complementary ways to connect those positions.
cnn-vs-transformer-why-conformer-needs-b.visual: Two ways to mix a sequence
cnn-vs-transformer-why-conformer-needs-b.caption: The highlighted query sees a fixed neighborhood through a convolution. Global self-attention can connect it directly to every position with input-dependent weights.

cards.title: Convolution
cards.text: Reuses a learned local kernel at each time position. Locality is built into the operation.

cards.title: Self-attention
cards.text: Computes routing weights from the current input. Useful context can come from anywhere in the sequence.

cards.title: Conformer
cards.text: Applies attention and local convolution within the same residual block, surrounded by feed-forward transforms.

cnn-vs-transformer-why-conformer-needs-b.note: Vanilla global attention forms pairwise scores with quadratic sequence-length size; a fixed-width convolution scales roughly linearly.
rows: Convolution supplies a useful local bias.
Self-attention supplies a short interaction path.
Combine the mechanisms and validate the actual trade-off.

inside-conformer-reason-behind-every-mod.idea: Transform each frame, exchange global context, refine local patterns, then transform again. The tensor returns to the same model width after every residual module.
inside-conformer-reason-behind-every-mod.visual: Follow one tensor through the block
inside-conformer-reason-behind-every-mod.caption: The two half-step FFNs surround attention and convolution. The convolution inset shows how channel mixing and time mixing are separated.

cards.title: Pointwise mixes channels
cards.text: A kernel of width 1 turns D features into 2D features independently at each time step.

cards.title: GLU chooses what passes
cards.text: Split the 2D features into A and B, then compute A ⊙ sigmoid(B), returning to width D.

cards.title: Depthwise mixes time
cards.text: Each channel has its own temporal kernel. A final pointwise projection recombines channels.

inside-conformer-reason-behind-every-mod.note: For D channels and kernel width k, a depthwise temporal convolution has kD weights; a full one has kD², excluding biases.
rows: Transforms features at one time position.
Gates channels and models local temporal evolution.
inside-conformer-reason-behind-every-mod.next_title: Why local and global context both matter

residual-vector-quantization-from-grids-.idea: Store a rough approximation, measure its error, and let the next codebook describe that error. Decode by adding the selected vectors.
residual-vector-quantization-from-grids-.caption: For x = (4.6, 2.3), the selected codewords sum to (4.55, 2.12). The final residual is (0.05, 0.18). The arrows are successive corrections, not nested grid cells.

cards.title: Codebook
cards.text: A shared table of vectors. An index is an address into that table.

cards.title: Residual
cards.text: Subtract the selected vector from the current error, then quantize what remains.

cards.title: Bitrate
cards.text: M codebooks with 256 entries use M bytes per vector, excluding the shared codebooks and other overhead.

residual-vector-quantization-from-grids-.note: Greedy stage-by-stage selection is efficient, but it does not guarantee the globally nearest additive combination.
rows: Add residual stages to encode corrections.
Use fewer active stages if the trained codec supports it.
Store MK vectors; there are up to Kᴹ index tuples, which may not all give unique sums.

conic-optimization-socp-sdp.idea: LP, SOCP, and SDP share a pattern: keep expressions affine and require them to belong to a cone. The cone defines what “nonnegative” means.
conic-optimization-socp-sdp.caption: The orthant constrains entries; a second-order cone bounds a norm; the PSD cone constrains every quadratic direction. The sketches are schematic.

cards.title: LP · Scalar positivity
cards.text: An affine slack vector must be componentwise nonnegative.

cards.title: SOCP · Norm bound
cards.text: A scalar must dominate the Euclidean length of a vector.

cards.title: SDP · Matrix positivity
cards.text: An affine symmetric matrix must be positive semidefinite. This is not entrywise positivity.

conic-optimization-socp-sdp.note: Use the smallest cone that expresses the model exactly. Greater representational power can cost more computation.
rows: A Euclidean norm below an affine bound
An affine symmetric matrix must be PSD

convex-quadratics-psd-schur-complement.idea: The Hessian determines curvature. Constraints determine which descent directions are available. At the optimum, no feasible direction improves the objective.
convex-quadratics-psd-schur-complement.visual: The best feasible point can sit on a boundary
convex-quadratics-psd-schur-complement.caption: For f(x, y) = (x − 2)² + (y − 2)² with 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 1, the unconstrained center is outside the box. The constrained optimum is (1, 1).

cards.title: PSD curvature
cards.text: For a symmetric quadratic, P ⪰ 0 makes the objective convex; P ≻ 0 makes it strictly convex.

cards.title: Feasible directions
cards.text: A nonzero gradient at a constrained optimum is possible: every allowed direction can still be uphill.

cards.title: Matrix reformulation
cards.text: With a positive definite leading block, the Schur complement converts a block PSD condition into a smaller one.

convex-quadratics-psd-schur-complement.note: For differentiable convex f over a convex feasible set, this condition is necessary and sufficient for optimality.
rows: A differentiable optimum has zero gradient.
Check the gradient against feasible directions.
Write x = x₀ + Fz using a basis F of the nullspace.

convex-sets-functions-first-order-geomet.idea: A convex set contains straight paths between its points. A convex function lies below its chords. A quasiconvex function only needs convex sublevel sets.
convex-sets-functions-first-order-geomet.caption: For f(x) = x², a chord sits above the curve. A tangent sits below it. These two pictures explain Jensen’s inequality and first-order lower bounds.

cards.title: Set test
cards.text: Can you join any two feasible points without leaving the set?

cards.title: Function test
cards.text: Does averaging inputs cost no more than averaging their function values?

cards.title: Quasiconvex test
cards.text: For every threshold t, is the set {x : f(x) ≤ t} convex? If yes, search over t with feasibility tests.

convex-sets-functions-first-order-geomet.note: Quasiconvexity replaces the right-hand average with max{f(x), f(y)}. It is a weaker requirement.
rows: Local minima are global; use convex optimization tools.
Bisection on the objective threshold may apply.
A ratio with an affine denominator
Keep the denominator strictly positive when forming its sublevel inequalities.

how-dinov2-dinov3-learn-without-labels.idea: The target comes from another view of the image and a slowly changing teacher. The student learns useful representations by matching those targets.
how-dinov2-dinov3-learn-without-labels.visual: The teacher supplies targets; the student learns
how-dinov2-dinov3-learn-without-labels.caption: Only the student receives gradients. Its EMA teacher sees global unmasked views; the student also sees local crops and masked patches. DINOv3 later anchors patch relationships to a Gram teacher.

cards.title: DINO · Global agreement
cards.text: Make different views agree at the image level, using teacher distributions over learned prototypes.

cards.title: iBOT + KoLeo · Detail & diversity
cards.text: Predict teacher patch targets at masked locations; use KoLeo to discourage crowded global features.

cards.title: DINOv3 · Preserve relationships
cards.text: Gram anchoring matches patch-to-patch similarities to a separate reference teacher during refinement.

how-dinov2-dinov3-learn-without-labels.note: The EMA teacher is a smoothed training history. Balanced, sharpened targets help prevent collapse; no human category label enters these losses.
rows: Dense features degrade during long training
DINOv3 adds Gram anchoring to preserve patch relationships.

weight-initialization-zero-xavier-he.idea: Randomness lets neurons learn different features. The right scale keeps activations and gradients usable as they pass through many layers.
weight-initialization-zero-xavier-he.visual: Small scale errors multiply with depth
weight-initialization-zero-xavier-he.caption: In a constant-width ReLU network, the approximate per-layer second-moment multiplier is r = n · Var(w) / 2. He initialization makes this multiplier about 1.

cards.title: Break symmetry
cards.text: Identical hidden units receive identical updates. Random weights give them different starting roles; biases can usually be zero.

cards.title: Match the activation
cards.text: Xavier balances fan-in and fan-out for linear or tanh-like propagation. He compensates for ReLU gating.

cards.title: Check both directions
cards.text: Forward signals depend on fan-in; backward signals also depend on fan-out and activation derivatives.

weight-initialization-zero-xavier-he.note: These are approximate starting scales, not convergence guarantees. Established architectures can require special gains and residual scaling.
rows: Start from Xavier; use the appropriate activation gain.
Use He/Kaiming with the matching negative slope.
An established Transformer or specialized model
